change-order-markup.formula: price = direct x (1 + OH%) x (1 + profit%); markup = price - direct; margin% = markup/price x 100.
change-order-markup.edition: The change-order overhead-and-profit markup (compounded) from construction estimating practice, by name (AIA G701 is the change-order form and prescribes no markup method; many public contracts set one markup per cost category, e.g. Caltrans labor 35% / equipment 15%, or cap a single markup, e.g. 10%).
change-order-markup.freeAccess: Overhead-and-profit markup on a change order is standard construction estimating; the allowed rate and method are in the contract.
change-order-markup.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
change-order-markup.editionNote: The change-order price with overhead and profit compounded: price = direct cost x (1 + overhead%) x (1 + profit%), where direct cost is labor + material + equipment for the added scope. The compounded method (overhead first, then profit) is common and yields slightly more than the additive direct x (1 + overhead% + profit%); which applies is set by the contract's general conditions. The reported margin is markup / price (gross margin), not the markup rate. This prices the change only; it does not evaluate schedule impact or a claim, and the contract terms and the owner's written approval govern.

assumptions.name: Compounded markup
assumptions.value: price = direct x (1 + OH%) x (1 + profit%)
assumptions.source: estimating practice; the contract governs (Caltrans CCO training 2020: per-category markups)

assumptions.name: Additive alternative
assumptions.value: direct x (1 + OH% + profit%) is slightly less; the contract decides

assumptions.name: Contract governs
assumptions.value: the general conditions set the allowed markup and method

weir-flow.formula: 90-degree V-notch: Q = 2.49*H^2.48. Rectangular Francis: Q = 3.33*(L-0.2H)*H^1.5 (contracted) or 3.33*L*H^1.5 (suppressed); with the approach width B and weir height P entered, Q = C L [(H + hv)^1.5 - hv^1.5], hv = V^2/(2g), V = Q/(B (P + H)), iterated. 1 cfs = 448.831 GPM.
weir-flow.edition: Per the USBR Water Measurement Manual (public domain) - V-notch and Francis rectangular-weir equations and Kindsvater-Carter / Francis coefficients, by name.
weir-flow.freeAccess: Free at usbr.gov/tsc/techreferences/mands/wmm; the user confirms the calibrated weir coefficient.
weir-flow.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
weir-flow.editionNote: Requires a sharp-crested, ventilated, free-flow weir; a submerged/drowned condition is invalid. Head below ~0.2 ft is low-accuracy. The optional approach-velocity correction (rectangular weirs, Francis velocity-head form, added 2026-10-09) matters for a low weir in a narrow channel; a V-notch is taken as fully contracted.

assumptions.name: Weir condition
assumptions.value: ventilated, sharp-crested, free-flow (fully contracted for the V-notch and contracted rectangular; end contractions suppressed for the suppressed rectangular)

oil-burner-firing-rate.formula: input_btu_hr = output_btu_hr / (steady_state_efficiency_pct / 100); firing_rate_gph = input_btu_hr / heating_value_btu_gal. No. 2 fuel oil heating value ~138,500 BTU/gal (editable).
oil-burner-firing-rate.edition: Oil burner nozzle firing rate (NORA / oil-heat industry practice; EIA No. 2 distillate heating value ~138,000-139,000 BTU/gal), by name; the appliance rating plate and firing range, the nozzle chart, the pump pressure, and a combustion analysis with the manufacturer's instructions govern.
oil-burner-firing-rate.freeAccess: The input-and-firing-rate conversion is a public physics identity (output over efficiency over heating value); the output, efficiency, and heating value are the appliance's and fuel's values.
oil-burner-firing-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
oil-burner-firing-rate.editionNote: When a service tech sizes or re-nozzles an oil burner, the firing rate in gallons per hour follows directly from the target heat output, the burner's efficiency, and the energy in the fuel. The heat OUTPUT the building needs is less than the fuel INPUT by the steady-state combustion efficiency, so the required input in BTU per hour is the output divided by that efficiency as a fraction. Dividing the input by the fuel's heating value in BTU per gallon gives the firing rate in gallons per hour. No. 2 fuel oil, the common heating oil, carries about 138,500 BTU per gallon, though the figure ranges roughly 138,000 to 140,000 depending on the blend, so it is left editable. To produce 88,000 BTU per hour of output at an 85% steady-state efficiency, the input is 88,000 divided by 0.85, or 103,529 BTU per hour, and the firing rate is 103,529 divided by 138,500, or 0.75 gallons per hour, pointing to a 0.75 GPH nozzle. Read the other direction, a 1.00 GPH nozzle fires 138,500 BTU per hour of input and, at 84% efficiency, delivers about 116,300 BTU per hour of output. Oil nozzles are manufactured in fixed GPH increments along with specific spray angles and patterns, so the calculated rate is rounded to the nearest available nozzle, and the actual delivered flow depends on the fuel-pump pressure: a nozzle is rated at 100 psi, and raising the pump pressure increases the flow in proportion to the square root of the pressure ratio. This is a sizing aid; the appliance's rating plate and its listed firing-rate range, the nozzle manufacturer's chart, the set pump pressure, and a proper combustion analysis performed per the manufacturer's instructions govern the final setup.

assumptions.name: Firing-rate conversion
assumptions.value: input = output / steady-state efficiency; GPH = input / heating value; No. 2 oil ~138,500 BTU/gal (editable)
assumptions.source: NORA / oil-heat practice; EIA distillate HHV

assumptions.name: Nozzle and pressure
assumptions.value: round to a stocked GPH nozzle and spray pattern; a nozzle is rated at 100 psi and flow scales with sqrt of the pressure ratio; a combustion analysis governs

irrigation-requirement.formula: ET_crop = Kc x ET0 x days. Net depth = max(0, ET_crop - effective rainfall). Gross depth = net / application efficiency. Total = gross_in x acres / 12 (acre-feet); gallons = acre-ft x 325,851.
irrigation-requirement.edition: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Crop Evapotranspiration, Allen et al. 1998) by name; USDA NRCS Irrigation Guide by name. Kc values from FAO 56 Table 12.
irrigation-requirement.freeAccess: FAO 56 free at fao.org; NRCS Irrigation Guide free at nrcs.usda.gov.
irrigation-requirement.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
irrigation-requirement.editionNote: Reference ET0 is user-supplied from the local CIMIS / Mesonet / NOAA station; the bundled Kc values are representative mid-season single values (the full FAO 56 dual-Kc method varies by growth stage). Verify against the local extension recommendation.

assumptions.name: Crop coefficient Kc
assumptions.value: alfalfa 0.95 season average (1.20 within one cutting), corn 1.20, cotton 1.15, wheat 1.15, pasture 0.95, turfgrass 0.95 cool season / 0.85 warm season, vegetables 1.05

assumptions.name: Application efficiency
assumptions.value: drip 90%, sprinkler 75%, flood 50%

assumptions.name: Acre-foot conversion
assumptions.value: 1 acre-foot = 325,851 US gallons

arc-flash-screen.formula: E_lee (cal/cm^2 at distance D in inches) = (7.935e-4 * V * I_bf * t) / D^2, with V in volts, I_bf in amps. The 7.935e-4 coefficient is the Lee (IEEE 1584) constant 2.142e6 (stated for kV, kA, mm and J/cm^2) re-expressed for volts, amps, inches and cal/cm^2: 2.142e6 / (1000 * 1000 * 25.4^2 * 4.184). Boundary distance D_b = sqrt((7.935e-4 * V * I_bf * t) / 1.2). PPE category band looked up against the NFPA 70E Table 130.7(C)(15)(c) ranges (table cited by name only; not reproduced).
arc-flash-screen.edition: NFPA 70E-2024 §130.5 governs the arc-flash risk assessment. IEEE 1584-2018 is the study-grade method.
arc-flash-screen.freeAccess: Free read-only access at nfpa.org/freeaccess. for NFPA 70E TOC and Annex D.
arc-flash-screen.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
arc-flash-screen.editionNote: Editions available: bundled PPE bands follow NFPA 70E-2024 Table 130.7(C)(15)(c) and the IEEE 1584-2018 method. Jurisdictions / employers on NFPA 70E-2021 differ at the margins; verify the edition adopted by your electrical-safety program.

assumptions.name: Equation source
assumptions.value: Ralph Lee 1982 closed-form, pre-IEEE-1584
assumptions.source: Lee, R.H., 'The Other Electrical Hazard: Electric Arc Blast Burns', IEEE Trans. on Industry Applications, 1982

assumptions.name: Second-degree threshold
assumptions.value: 1.2 cal/cm^2

assumptions.name: Conservatism
assumptions.value: Lee is conservative below 600 V open-air but may be non-conservative for some 480 V box configurations covered by IEEE 1584

assumptions.name: PPE category bands
assumptions.value: 1.2 / 4 / 8 / 25 / 40 cal/cm^2 breakpoints
assumptions.source: NFPA 70E Table 130.7(C)(15)(c) ranges; table not reproduced

rebar-schedule.formula: Cut length = straight_ft + bend_allowance_in / 12 where bend_allowance = sum over bend types of (multiplier × bar_diameter): 90° = 6 db, 135° = 6 db, 180° = 4 db, stirrup = 14 db, hook = 6 db. Row weight = cut_length × unit_weight × pieces. Total = sum of rows.
rebar-schedule.edition: ACI 318-19 / CRSI Manual of Standard Practice by name. Unit weights per CRSI / ASTM A615 published values: #3 = 0.376 lb/ft, ..., #11 = 5.313 lb/ft.
rebar-schedule.freeAccess: ACI 318 + CRSI manuals licensed; ASTM A615 nominal-weight table free in published engineering references.
rebar-schedule.governance: Estimate. Engineer of record governs the design and acceptance. Verify against the project structural drawings and the manufacturer's published capacity / chart.
rebar-schedule.editionNote: Single-edition (CRSI standard practice; bar-diameter and weight tables stable across editions).

assumptions.name: Unit-weight table
assumptions.value: data/construction/rebar-unit-weights.json keyed to bar size

assumptions.name: Bar-diameter table
assumptions.value: data/construction/rebar-unit-weights.json keyed to bar size

recirc-loop-sizing.formula: q_per_ft = U * (T_hot - T_ambient). Q_total = q_per_ft * L. GPM = Q_total / (500 * set-point-delta). Friction head via Hazen-Williams (C=140 for copper). Pump-size ladder: 1/40 / 1/25 / 1/20 / 1/12 / 1/6 / 1/4 HP, with 25% wet-rotor wire-to-water efficiency factor.
recirc-loop-sizing.edition: ASPE Data Book Vol. 4 (Plumbing Engineering Design Handbook) Chapter 6 simplified per-foot heat-loss method. ASHRAE 90.1-2022 §7.4.4 for recirculation control.
recirc-loop-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
recirc-loop-sizing.editionNote: Per-foot loss coefficients are operator-grade defaults that match ASPE Data Book Vol. 4 Ch. 6 simplified per-foot losses for copper pipe at typical residential conditions. AHJ governs.

assumptions.name: Pipe material
assumptions.value: Type L copper

assumptions.name: Loss-coefficient table
assumptions.value: U (Btu/hr/ft/°F-delta) by nominal size (0.5 / 0.75 / 1 / 1.25 / 1.5 in) and insulation thickness (0 / 0.5 / 1 / 1.5 in)
assumptions.source: ASPE Data Book Vol. 4 Ch. 6 simplified per-foot losses

assumptions.name: Insulation interpolation
assumptions.value: linear in insulation thickness between bundled break points

assumptions.name: Pump efficiency
assumptions.value: 25% wire-to-water for small wet-rotor circulators
assumptions.source: manufacturer typical (Taco / Grundfos / Bell & Gossett small circulators)

assumptions.name: Pump-size ladder
assumptions.value: 1/40, 1/25, 1/20, 1/12, 1/6, 1/4 HP next-standard rounding
assumptions.source: common North American residential / light-commercial circulator sizes

assumptions.name: Length floor
assumptions.value: loops below 50 ft warned: 'may not need recirc; consider point-of-use heater'

assumptions.name: Insulation floor
assumptions.value: 0-in insulation flagged as non-compliant for most ASHRAE 90.1 jurisdictions

gas-leak-hole-diameter.formula: d = sqrt( 4 Q / (8706 x c x pi x sqrt(dP / SG)) ), the inverse of Q = 8706 x c x (pi d^2 / 4) x sqrt(dP / SG); orifice area A = Q / (8706 c sqrt(dP/SG)).
gas-leak-hole-diameter.edition: Classical orifice-flow leak approximation (incompressible, small leak at low pressure), solved for the diameter; the 8706 coefficient is the orifice equation in these units (25 sqrt(2 x 144 x 32.174 / 0.0764)); gas specific gravity bundled.
gas-leak-hole-diameter.freeAccess: The orifice-flow leak relation is public; the gas specific gravity is a bundled property.
gas-leak-hole-diameter.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
gas-leak-hole-diameter.editionNote: Single-edition (physics). The equivalent orifice (hole) diameter for a measured gas leak, the inverse of Q = 8706 c A sqrt(dP/SG). This is the small-leak orifice-flow approximation (incompressible, low-pressure) and gives an ESTIMATE of the effective hole size, not a code leak-test method. The discharge coefficient (0.7 default for a rough crack; about 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice) and the actual crack geometry, temperature, and choked flow at high pressure ratios all shift it. Distinct from the water orifice-diameter tile, which inverts the incompressible Q = Cd A sqrt(2 g h) form. Any positive leak is a hazard: find and repair it, and follow the code test and the utility's procedure.

assumptions.name: Discharge coefficient c
assumptions.value: 0.7 default for a rough-edged crack or fitting leak; a sharp-edged orifice is about 0.6 (Eclipse prints 0.60)

assumptions.name: Gas specific gravity
assumptions.value: bundled natural-gas / propane specific gravity

assumptions.name: Estimate only
assumptions.value: the small-leak orifice approximation, not a code leak-test method

osha-top10.formula: (reference page; no compute) Most-recently published OSHA Top 10 Most Frequently Cited Standards, listed by 29 CFR section number with topic.
osha-top10.edition: OSHA-published top-10 list (refreshed annually each fiscal year).
osha-top10.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
osha-top10.editionNote: Single-edition (refreshed annually from OSHA's published top-10 list).

seer-eer.formula: EER = BTU/hr ÷ W (steady state at AHRI 95 °F outdoor / 80 °F indoor). SEER weights cooling capacity over an AHRI 210/240 seasonal bin profile. SEER2 / EER2 add return-static loading per the 2023 federal test procedure.
seer-eer.edition: AHRI 210/240-2023 by name. DOE 10 CFR 430 (federal energy-conservation standards) by section.
seer-eer.freeAccess: AHRI 210/240 licensed; DOE 10 CFR 430 free at ecfr.gov.
seer-eer.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
seer-eer.editionNote: Editions available: AHRI 210/240-2023 is the current edition (SEER2 / EER2). Older equipment rated per AHRI 210/240-2008 (SEER / EER) is shown alongside.

assumptions.name: Test conditions
assumptions.value: AHRI 95 °F outdoor / 80 °F indoor / 67 °F wet bulb

assumptions.name: SEER-EER relation
assumptions.value: EER = -0.02 SEER^2 + 1.12 SEER (Wassmer 2003, NREL Building America House Simulation Protocols); a nameplate EER governs

combustion-air-max-input.formula: Standard volume method solved for input (inverse of combustion-air): max appliance BTU/hr = (room_volume_ft3 / 50) * 1000, since IFGC 2021 §304.5 treats a space as adequate at 50 ft^3 per 1000 BTU/hr.
combustion-air-max-input.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
combustion-air-max-input.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow IFGC 2021 / NFPA 54-2021. IFGC 2027 is the current published edition and 2024 preceded it; jurisdictions on any of these differ at the margins; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Standard method
assumptions.value: IFGC §304.5 volume rule; above the returned input the space is confined and needs openings, or use the known-air-infiltration-rate method (§304.5.2), or outdoor openings (§304.6)

bend-allowance.formula: BA = (π / 180) × angle × (R + K × t) where K is the K-factor (neutral-axis offset) and t is sheet thickness; outside setback OSSB = (R + t) × tan(angle / 2); bend deduction BD = 2 × OSSB - BA; flat blank = leg1 + leg2 - BD with both legs measured to the outside mold line.
bend-allowance.edition: Machinery's Handbook by name; SME Sheet Metal Forming by name.
bend-allowance.freeAccess: Older Machinery's Handbook editions free at archive.org.
bend-allowance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

assumptions.name: Default K-factor
assumptions.value: 0.44 unless the user supplies the shop's own (the neutral axis sits between 0 and 0.5 t)
assumptions.source: sheet-metal practice; SendCutSend bend guide prints K .43

reverse-curve.formula: parallel tangents: both arcs sweep the same central angle I = arccos(1 - p/(R1+R2)) for a perpendicular offset p; T = R tan(I/2) and L = R I_rad per arc; tangent-point distance = (R1+R2) sin I.
reverse-curve.edition: Reverse (S) curve geometry between parallel tangents per Ghilani & Wolf, Elementary Surveying, and the AASHTO A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets (the Green Book), by name; first-principles circular-curve trig.
reverse-curve.freeAccess: The reverse-curve offset geometry (equal central angle from the tangent offset, semi-tangents, arc lengths) is standard published route-surveying math; the design of record and the engineer of record govern the alignment.
reverse-curve.governance: Estimate. Engineer of record governs the design and acceptance. Verify against the project structural drawings and the manufacturer's published capacity / chart.
reverse-curve.editionNote: A reverse (S) curve: two circular arcs of opposite curvature meeting at a point of reverse curvature (PRC), the geometry of a railroad crossover or a lane shift that returns the alignment to a line parallel to where it began. Because the outgoing tangent must end up parallel to the incoming one, both arcs sweep the same central angle I, found from the perpendicular offset between the two parallel tangents: p = (R1 + R2)(1 - cos I), so I = arccos(1 - p/(R1 + R2)). Each arc then has its semi-tangent T = R tan(I/2) and arc length L = R I (radians), and the two tangent points are (R1 + R2) sin I apart along the tangent direction. With equal radii the two arcs are mirror images. A reverse curve gives no room to run out superelevation between the arcs, so AASHTO and AREMA want a tangent (or spiral) inserted at the PRC on anything but low speeds. A design aid; AASHTO/AREMA and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Equal central angle
assumptions.value: I = arccos(1 - p/(R1+R2)); both arcs sweep I so the tangents stay parallel

assumptions.name: Semi-tangents and lengths
assumptions.value: T = R tan(I/2); L = R I_rad per arc; tangent-point distance (R1+R2) sin I

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: opposite-curvature arcs between parallel tangents; insert a tangent/spiral at the PRC for superelevation runout

commercial-lighting-load.formula: lighting_va = area x unit load (Table 220.42(A)); recep_va = straps x 180 VA (220.14(I)); recep_demand = recep_va <= 10 kVA ? recep_va : 10000 + 0.50 x (recep_va - 10000) (220.47); total = lighting + recep_demand; amps = total / (sqrt(3) x V line-to-line) three-phase, total / V single-phase.
commercial-lighting-load.edition: Commercial general-lighting and receptacle load, NEC 2023 Table 220.42(A), 220.14(I), and 220.47 (Table 220.12 and 220.44 in 2020 and earlier), by name.
commercial-lighting-load.freeAccess: NEC is free to read at nfpa.org/freeaccess. The Table 220.42(A) unit loads already include the 125% continuous-load multiplier of 210.20(A) (the table footnote), so no second 125% is added; the energy code may set the lighting unit load.
commercial-lighting-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
commercial-lighting-load.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Unit and strap loads
assumptions.value: the general-lighting unit load is from Table 220.42(A) by occupancy; each general-use receptacle strap counts at 180 VA

assumptions.name: Continuous multiplier
assumptions.value: the 125% continuous-load multiplier (210.20(A)) is already in the Table 220.42(A) unit loads, so it is not applied again (an office is 1.3 VA/ft2)

assumptions.name: Receptacle demand
assumptions.value: 100% of the first 10 kVA of receptacle load plus 50% of the remainder

shock-approach-boundary.formula: lookup by nominal phase-to-phase AC voltage band: limited approach (exposed movable conductor vs exposed fixed circuit part) and restricted approach; below 50 V no boundary is specified.
shock-approach-boundary.edition: AC shock approach boundaries, NFPA 70E-2024 Table 130.4, by name.
shock-approach-boundary.freeAccess: NFPA 70E is free to read at nfpa.org/freeaccess. These are shock boundaries only; the arc-flash boundary is a separate determination. Crossing the restricted approach requires a qualified person, an energized-work permit, and shock PPE.
shock-approach-boundary.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
shock-approach-boundary.editionNote: Single-edition (NFPA 70E-2024 Table 130.4; refresh on the next 70E cycle).

assumptions.name: Limited approach
assumptions.value: the boundary an unqualified person must not cross; the larger distance applies to an exposed movable conductor, the smaller to an exposed fixed circuit part

assumptions.name: Restricted approach
assumptions.value: the boundary requiring a qualified person, an energized-work permit, and shock PPE to cross

overflow-scupper-sizing.formula: Q = 3.33 L H^1.5 (cfs, L and H in ft); contracted Q = 3.33 (L - 0.2 H) H^1.5; gpm = cfs x 448.83.
overflow-scupper-sizing.edition: The rectangular (Francis) weir capacity of an overflow scupper, secondary roof drainage per IPC 1108 / FM Global, by name. The IPC's scupper sizing figure (Figure 1106.5 in the 2015 IPC, as adopted in the 2018 NC Plumbing Code) prints the contracted form Q = 3.33 (L - 0.2 H) H^1.5 with H measured 6 ft back from the opening; the suppressed value is the full-channel-width case.
overflow-scupper-sizing.freeAccess: The Francis rectangular-weir formula is public; the secondary-drainage requirement is in the published IPC (Section 1108) and FM Global data sheets.
overflow-scupper-sizing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
overflow-scupper-sizing.editionNote: Overflow (secondary) scupper capacity treated as a rectangular sharp-crested weir: Q = 3.33 L H^1.5 in cfs with the length L and the head H in feet, or the end-contracted form 3.33 (L - 0.2 H) H^1.5 for a scupper narrower than the wall. The head H is the depth of water above the scupper invert at the design condition, which for secondary drainage is evaluated with the primary drains assumed blocked (IPC 1108 / FM Global); the overflow path must pass the design storm on its own. This sizes the weir flow; it does not set the invert height, the number of scuppers, or the resulting ponding depth for the structural roof-load check. A design aid; the plumbing code, the AHJ, and the structural engineer govern.

assumptions.name: Weir flow
assumptions.value: Q = 3.33 L H^1.5 (cfs, ft); contracted 3.33 (L - 0.2 H) H^1.5

assumptions.name: Blocked-primary head
assumptions.value: H evaluated with the primary drainage assumed plugged

assumptions.name: Structural check separate
assumptions.value: the ponding depth and roof load are the structural engineer's

unit-cost-earthwork.formula: hourly_cost = equipment_rate_per_hr + operator_rate_per_hr + support_rate_per_hr; unit_cost_per_cy = hourly_cost / production_cy_per_hr; total_cost = unit_cost_per_cy x total_cy.
unit-cost-earthwork.edition: Production unit-cost identity by name (unit cost = hourly cost / production); first-principles cost arithmetic.
unit-cost-earthwork.freeAccess: The unit-cost arithmetic is public first-principles; the hourly rates come from the cost records and the production from the production tiles.
unit-cost-earthwork.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
unit-cost-earthwork.editionNote: The equipment rate is the ownership-plus-operating rate from equipment-hourly-rate or the machine's cost records; the production comes from the production tiles. Low production (soft ground, long haul, poor match) is what blows up the unit price - the number to attack is the production, not the rate.

assumptions.name: Hourly rates
assumptions.value: equipment ownership + operating, operator wage + burden, and support, from the cost records

assumptions.name: Production
assumptions.value: the hourly production rate from the production tiles (dozer, haul-cycle, loader)

dumpster-count.formula: by_vol = ceil(debris_cy / (container_cy x fill_efficiency)); by_wt = ceil(debris_tons / weight_cap_tons); hauls = max(by_vol, by_wt).
dumpster-count.edition: Roll-off haul-count identity by name (the greater of the volume-limited and weight-limited counts); first-principles governing-constraint arithmetic.
dumpster-count.freeAccess: The governing-constraint logic is public first-principles; the container size and weight cap come from the hauler.
dumpster-count.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dumpster-count.editionNote: The debris volume and weight come from demo-debris; the container size and weight cap come from the hauler. Heavy debris such as concrete and masonry hits the weight cap first, light debris the volume. The fill efficiency is below one for bulky debris; overweight boxes are a haul-back.

assumptions.name: Container
assumptions.value: roll-off box size (~30 cy) and weight cap (~8 tons) from the hauler

assumptions.name: Fill efficiency
assumptions.value: usable fraction of the box, below one for bulky debris (~0.7 default)

spray-drift-buffer.formula: Buffer = base buffer x (wind / 10 mph) x (release height / reference height). Base buffer set by droplet class: Very Coarse 5, Coarse 10, Medium 20, Fine 40 ft (editable, representative).
spray-drift-buffer.edition: USDA / land-grant extension drift-management guidance; EPA pesticide label and the Worker Protection Standard (40 CFR 170), by name.
spray-drift-buffer.freeAccess: Extension drift-management guidance free on land-grant university extension sites. The label ships with the product.
spray-drift-buffer.governance: Read and follow the product label. The label is the law (FIFRA).
spray-drift-buffer.editionNote: This is a RELATIVE planning aid, not the label's required buffer, which is the law (FIFRA). The droplet-class base buffers are editable representative values, not regulatory numbers.

assumptions.name: Droplet-class base buffers
assumptions.value: 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 ft for Very Coarse / Coarse / Medium / Fine at the 10 mph, 20 in reference; editable

assumptions.name: Label governs
assumptions.value: do not spray toward a sensitive area, during a temperature inversion, or above the label's maximum wind speed; coarser droplets and a lower boom cut drift far more than any buffer

fatigue-notch-sensitivity.formula: sqrt(a) [sqrt(in)] = 0.246 - 3.08e-3 Sut + 1.51e-5 Sut^2 - 2.67e-8 Sut^3 (bending/axial) or 0.190 - 2.51e-3 Sut + 1.35e-5 Sut^2 - 2.67e-8 Sut^3 (torsion), Sut in kpsi; q = 1/(1 + sqrt(a)/sqrt(r)); Kf = 1 + q (Kt - 1).
fatigue-notch-sensitivity.edition: Neuber's notch-sensitivity equation with the steel Neuber constants (Shigley, Mischke and Budynas, Mechanical Engineering Design, Ch. 6, Eqs. 6-32 to 6-35), by name; it reproduces Shigley Example 6-6 (Sut 690 MPa = 100 kpsi, r = 3 mm, Kt = 1.65: sqrt(a) = 0.0622 sqrt(in), Kf = 1.55).
fatigue-notch-sensitivity.freeAccess: Standard published fatigue relations; Kt (from a chart), the notch radius, and the strength are the user's inputs.
fatigue-notch-sensitivity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fatigue-notch-sensitivity.editionNote: The fatigue stress-concentration factor a steel part actually feels at a notch: Kf = 1 + q (Kt - 1), with q from the notch radius and the ultimate strength. Kt is read from a stress-concentration chart for the geometry; this does not compute it. Steel with Sut 50 to 250 kpsi, the range of the Neuber-constant fits. A design aid; test data govern.

assumptions.name: Notch sensitivity
assumptions.value: Neuber q = 1/(1 + sqrt(a)/sqrt(r))

assumptions.name: Neuber constant
assumptions.value: cubic fits in Sut (kpsi) for bending/axial and torsion, steel

assumptions.name: Kt
assumptions.value: entered from a chart (Peterson; Shigley Table A-15)

band-brake-torque.formula: theta in radians; T1 = T2 e^(mu theta); tension ratio = e^(mu theta); T_brake = (T1 - T2) r.
band-brake-torque.edition: The Eytelwein / capstan belt-friction relation T1 = T2 e^(mu theta) and the band-brake torque T = (T1 - T2) r (Shigley, Mechanical Engineering Design, Ch. 16; capstan equation), by name.
band-brake-torque.freeAccess: The capstan/Eytelwein relation and the band-brake torque are standard published mechanics results; the tensions, wrap angle, friction, and drum radius are the user's inputs.
band-brake-torque.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
band-brake-torque.editionNote: Band brake / capstan torque from the Eytelwein (belt-friction) relation T1 = T2 e^(mu theta): the tight-side tension T1 grows exponentially from the applied slack-side tension T2 with the friction mu and the wrap angle theta (radians), and the braking torque on the drum is T = (T1 - T2) r. The ratio e^(mu theta) climbs fast with wrap - a 270-degree wrap at mu 0.3 multiplies the pull by 4.1, a full turn by 6.6 - which is why a couple of turns of rope on a bollard hold a boat and a light lever pull stops a heavy drum. A band brake whose anchored end is the tight side is self-energizing (rotation tightens it). With the band width it gives the peak lining pressure at the tight end, p_max = T1/(b r), and with the thickness the band tension stress T1/(b t) (added 2026-10-09); the lever geometry that sets the actuating force, the self-energizing sign, and the heat of braking are separate; the friction coefficient is the user's (band lining on the drum). A design aid; Shigley and the brake maker govern.

assumptions.name: Eytelwein
assumptions.value: T1 = T2 e^(mu theta), theta the wrap angle in radians

assumptions.name: Brake torque
assumptions.value: T = (T1 - T2) r on the drum

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: tension ratio, torque, and (with the band width and thickness) peak lining pressure and band stress; lever geometry, self-energizing, and heat are separate

pool-heater-btu.formula: Q_btu = gallons x 8.34 x dT; delivered = nameplate input x eff (the output key holds the INPUT rating); hours = Q_btu / delivered.
pool-heater-btu.edition: The sensible water-heating relation (1 Btu raises 1 lb of water 1 F), by name.
pool-heater-btu.freeAccess: The water-heating energy relation and the 8.34 lb/gal constant are standard published values. The equipment ratings and site conditions govern.
pool-heater-btu.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pool-heater-btu.editionNote: The pool heat-up: energy Btu = gallons x 8.34 lb/gal x temperature rise, and the heat-up time = energy / (heater nameplate input x efficiency). A gas heater at ~80% warms fast; a heat pump (entered as its heat output with efficiency 1.0) is far slower but cheaper to run, so it is left on to hold temperature rather than for a quick warm-up. This returns the sensible heat-up only: it ignores the cover, evaporation, and standby losses, so real heat-up takes longer, and it does not size the gas line or verify the electrical service. A sizing estimate; the equipment ratings and site conditions govern.

assumptions.name: Sensible heat
assumptions.value: Btu = gallons x 8.34 x dT; 1 Btu raises 1 lb water 1 F

assumptions.name: Heat-up time
assumptions.value: hours = energy / (output x efficiency); for a heat pump enter its heat output in Btu/h with efficiency 1.0, not its COP

assumptions.name: No standby loss
assumptions.value: ignores cover/evaporation/standby losses; real heat-up runs longer

fence-estimate.formula: Sections = ceil(run / spacing); posts = sections + 1; rails = sections x rails/section; pickets = ceil(run x 12 / (picket width + gap)).
fence-estimate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fence-estimate.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice / first-principles take-off; refresh as practice and product data shift).

assumptions.name: End-post rule
assumptions.value: straight run posts = sections + 1; corners/ends/gates added by eye

spindle-power-torque.formula: Cutting horsepower = MRR (in3/min) x unit power (hp per in3/min); motor horsepower = cutting hp / (efficiency / 100); spindle torque (lb-ft) = 5252 x cutting hp / rpm.
spindle-power-torque.edition: Cutting power and spindle torque - first-principles specific-cutting-energy relation with Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press) unit-power values, by name; the 5252 torque constant is universal.
spindle-power-torque.freeAccess: The specific-cutting-energy arithmetic is public; the material removal rate, unit power, efficiency, and rpm are user-supplied.
spindle-power-torque.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
spindle-power-torque.editionNote: First-principles specific-cutting-energy relation. The unit-power (specific cutting energy) values are Machinery's Handbook tabular references (about 1.0 hp per in3/min carbon steel, 0.33 aluminum, 1.5 stainless/titanium); the tool, sharpness, and machine govern the real draw -- this is the stall / motor-size check before a heavy cut.

assumptions.name: Unit power
assumptions.value: specific cutting energy, hp per in3/min: ~1.0 carbon steel, ~0.33 aluminum, ~1.5 stainless/titanium; default 1.0

assumptions.name: Drive efficiency
assumptions.value: spindle drive efficiency; default 80%

track-superelevation.formula: equilibrium E = 0.0007 x D x V squared (in, degrees of curve, mph); unbalance = equilibrium - actual; maximum speed = sqrt((actual + allowable unbalance) / (0.0007 x D)); elevation required for a target speed = equilibrium at target - allowable unbalance.
track-superelevation.edition: The classic equilibrium-elevation relation for a circular curve at steady speed, by name, with 49 CFR 213 (FRA Track Safety Standards) named as the source of the elevation and unbalance limits. The caps are entered rather than reproduced. The railroad's engineering instructions and timetable special instructions, and the track owner, govern.
track-superelevation.freeAccess: 49 CFR 213 is US federal regulation and public domain; the elevation relation is standard track engineering arithmetic on the user's own curve.
track-superelevation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
track-superelevation.editionNote: Equilibrium elevation is the bank at which the resultant force sits square in the track and nothing pushes sideways on either rail. Below it the train leans out and loads the high rail; above it, at low speed, it leans in and loads the low rail. Freight railroads deliberately underelevate for that reason, because a curve elevated for a fast train punishes a slow one, and low-rail wear and the risk of a slow train stringlining are both real consequences. That is why the operating rule is written on UNBALANCE rather than on elevation: actual elevation is set for the mixed traffic that uses the curve, and the maximum speed is whatever that elevation plus the allowed unbalance supports. Raising the elevation to permit a faster passenger train makes the slow freight worse, and the limits on both are what keep that trade inside safe bounds. The field version is the two-question form -- what is the maximum speed for this curve as elevated, and what elevation would this curve need for a target speed -- and both are answered from the same coefficient. What this does not do is design a curve. Spiral transition length is what allows elevation to be run in and out, it usually governs whether a given elevation is achievable at all, and elevation cannot be applied without adequate spirals.

assumptions.name: The rule is written on unbalance
assumptions.value: actual elevation serves mixed traffic; speed follows elevation plus the allowed unbalance

assumptions.name: Caps are entered, not shipped
assumptions.value: actual elevation commonly capped near 6 in in railroad practice (FRA 213.57(a) allows up to 8 in on Classes 1-2 and 7 in on Classes 3-5) and unbalance near 3 in, with more only by specific approval for specific equipment

assumptions.name: Spirals govern achievability
assumptions.value: elevation cannot be applied without adequate transition length to run it in and out

wind-solid-sign.formula: F = qh G Cf As; Case B eccentric moment M = F x 0.2 x B.
wind-solid-sign.edition: The ASCE 7-22 Section 29.3 design wind force on solid freestanding walls and signs, F = qh G Cf As, with Cf from Figure 29.3-1, by name.
wind-solid-sign.freeAccess: ASCE 7 is available through the ASCE Library at ascelibrary.org; the Section 29.3 provisions are public.
wind-solid-sign.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wind-solid-sign.editionNote: Cf here is a net two-face force coefficient from Figure 29.3-1 as a function of the aspect ratio B/s and the clearance ratio s/h (not the +/- GCp of a building wall); it rises for tall, narrow signs. Case B applies the resultant at a 0.2B eccentricity (the torsion that sizes the post and footing) and a wide sign (B/s >= 2) adds a Case C strip loading. A design aid, not the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Net force coefficient
assumptions.value: Cf ~1.2-2.0 from Fig 29.3-1 by B/s and s/h; net two-face, not building-wall GCp

assumptions.name: Case B eccentricity
assumptions.value: the resultant acts at 0.2B, producing the torsion that sizes the post and footing

condenser-heat-rejection.formula: Q_btuh = (unit == tons) ? Q x 12,000 : Q; W_comp = Q_btuh/COP; THR = Q_btuh (1 + 1/COP); factor = 1 + 1/COP; THR_tons = THR/12,000.
condenser-heat-rejection.edition: The condenser total heat of rejection THR = Q_evap + W_comp = Q_evap (1 + 1/COP), a standard refrigeration-cycle result, by name.
condenser-heat-rejection.freeAccess: The total-heat-of-rejection relation is a public refrigeration-cycle result; the ASHRAE Handbook covers condenser sizing.
condenser-heat-rejection.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
condenser-heat-rejection.editionNote: The total heat of rejection THR = Q_evap + W_comp = Q_evap (1 + 1/COP), the compressor work W_comp = Q_evap/COP, and the typical heat-rejection factor of about 1.25 for comfort cooling (higher at lower COP / low-temperature refrigeration). This returns the total heat of rejection at the condenser from the evaporator load and the COP - it uses the compressor work implied by the COP, assumes the condenser rejects the full evaporator-plus-compressor heat (no desuperheater/heat-recovery split), and it counts all of the compressor input as reaching the condenser, which is right for a hermetic or suction-cooled compressor (its motor heat goes into the refrigerant); an open or belt-drive compressor rejects its motor losses to the room, so its THR is slightly lower. Until 2026-09-26 this sentence had the hermetic and open-drive cases reversed. An engineering aid; the equipment's rated heat-of-rejection data govern.

assumptions.name: Heat of rejection
assumptions.value: THR = Q_evap (1 + 1/COP), the evaporator load plus the compressor work

assumptions.name: Rejection factor
assumptions.value: 1 + 1/COP, about 1.25 for comfort cooling, higher at lower COP

assumptions.name: No heat recovery
assumptions.value: full rejection at the condenser; no desuperheater split or external motor heat

culvert-inlet-control.formula: Inlet control HW/D (circular barrel): unsubmerged Form 1 HW/D = Hc/D + K[Q/(A sqrt D)]^M + Ks S; submerged HW/D = c[Q/(A sqrt D)]^2 + Y + Ks S; Ks = -0.5 (mitered +0.7). Barrel A = pi D^2/4; critical depth from g A^3 = Q^2 T on the circular segment, Hc = dc + Vc^2/2g. HW = (HW/D) D.
culvert-inlet-control.edition: FHWA HDS-5, Hydraulic Design of Highway Culverts, 3rd ed. (FHWA-HIF-12-026, 2012), Appendix A equations A.1 and A.3 and the Table A.1 constants for circular concrete and corrugated-metal pipe, by name; the equation assembly and slope term verified against the HDS-5 Appendix A worked values, and the circular critical-depth solve against the Froude = 1 definition.
culvert-inlet-control.freeAccess: HDS-5 is a public-domain FHWA publication (FHWA-HIF-12-026); the inlet-control equations and the Table A.1 constants are reproduced from it. Diameter, discharge, slope, and the inlet configuration are the user's inputs.
culvert-inlet-control.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
culvert-inlet-control.editionNote: FHWA HDS-5 culvert headwater by INLET control for a circular barrel: the inlet - its size, shape, and edge - not the barrel length or the outlet, sets the ponding depth. Two regimes: unsubmerged at low flow (the inlet acts like a weir) uses HW/D = Hc/D + K[Q/(A sqrt D)]^M + Ks S, with the specific head at critical depth Hc = dc + Vc^2/2g found by iterating the circular-segment geometry (A = (D^2/8)(theta - sin theta), T = D sin(theta/2)); submerged at high flow (the inlet acts like an orifice) uses HW/D = c[Q/(A sqrt D)]^2 + Y + Ks S; between flow factors 3.5 and 4.0 the two are blended. Ks = -0.5 (mitered inlets +0.7) is the barrel-slope correction, and the K, M, c, Y constants are the HDS-5 Table A.1 values for the chosen shape and inlet edge. The ACTUAL headwater is the GREATER of inlet and outlet control - outlet control (barrel friction, tailwater, length) is a separate calculation - so this is one of two checks, not the final answer. HW is measured above the inlet invert. A design aid; the HDS-5 nomographs themselves carry about +/-10%, and the engineer of record and the DOT drainage manual govern.

assumptions.name: Unsubmerged Form 1
assumptions.value: HW/D = Hc/D + K[Q/(A sqrt D)]^M + Ks S; Hc from the circular critical depth

assumptions.name: Submerged
assumptions.value: HW/D = c[Q/(A sqrt D)]^2 + Y + Ks S, above flow factor ~4.0

assumptions.name: Slope / scope
assumptions.value: Ks = -0.5 (mitered +0.7); circular barrels only; inlet control only (outlet control is a separate check)

concrete-longterm-defl.formula: xi = 2.0 (>=60 mo) / 1.4 (>=12) / 1.2 (>=6) / 1.0 (else); lambda = xi / (1 + 50 rho'); additional = lambda x immediate; total = immediate + additional.
concrete-longterm-defl.edition: The ACI 318-19 24.2.4.1.1 additional time-dependent (creep and shrinkage) deflection multiplier lambda = xi / (1 + 50 rho'), with the 24.2.4.1.3 time factor xi, by name.
concrete-longterm-defl.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; the 24.2.4 deflection provisions are in the published code.
concrete-longterm-defl.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
concrete-longterm-defl.editionNote: The ACI 318-19 24.2.4.1.1 additional time-dependent deflection multiplier lambda = xi / (1 + 50 rho'), with the 24.2.4.1.3 time factor xi (2.0 at 5 years or more, 1.4 at 12 months, 1.2 at 6 months, 1.0 at 3 months), the additional long-term deflection = lambda x immediate, and the total = immediate + additional. The multiplier applies to the immediate deflection from the SUSTAINED portion of the load (dead plus the sustained fraction of live). Compression reinforcement rho' = As'/(b d) reduces creep, so a doubly-reinforced beam deflects far less over time. The total long-term deflection is what the L/240 and L/480 serviceability limits are checked against; the immediate deflection itself comes from an effective-moment-of-inertia (Ie) analysis. A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record's design.

assumptions.name: Time factor
assumptions.value: xi = 2.0 at 5 years or more, 1.4 at 12 months, 1.2 at 6 months, 1.0 at 3 months

assumptions.name: Compression steel
assumptions.value: rho' = As'/(b d) reduces the multiplier; a doubly-reinforced beam creeps far less

assumptions.name: Sustained load
assumptions.value: the multiplier applies to the immediate deflection from the sustained load only

rc-slender-column-magnify.formula: Cm = 0.6 - 0.4 M1/M2 (ACI 318-19 Eq. 6.6.4.5.3a; M1/M2 negative for single curvature, positive for double, no lower bound); Pc = pi^2 EI / (k lu)^2; delta_ns = max(Cm/(1 - Pu/(0.75 Pc)), 1.0); Mc = max(delta_ns M2, M2,min), M2,min = Pu(0.6 + 0.03 h).
rc-slender-column-magnify.edition: The ACI 318-19 Section 6.6.4.5 nonsway (braced) slender-column moment magnifier, by name.
rc-slender-column-magnify.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; the Section 6.6.4 slenderness provisions are in the published code.
rc-slender-column-magnify.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rc-slender-column-magnify.editionNote: The critical buckling load Pc carries a 0.75 stiffness reduction in the magnifier denominator; the design moment is floored at M2,min = Pu(0.6 + 0.03h); a column just over the slenderness limit k lu/r <= 34 + 12(M1/M2) (ACI 318-19 Eq. 6.2.5.1b) picks up an amplifier the flexure check never applies; in ACI 318-19, M1/M2 is negative for single curvature (Cm up to 1.0) and positive for double curvature (lowering Cm, to 0.2 at M1 = M2), the reverse of the pre-2014 sign convention. This is the nonsway (braced-frame) magnifier only. A design aid, not the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Nonsway frame
assumptions.value: braced (nonsway) 6.6.4.5 magnifier; a sway frame uses the 6.6.4.6 delta_s procedure

assumptions.name: 0.75 stiffness factor
assumptions.value: Pc appears as 0.75 Pc in the denominator (the stiffness-reduction factor)

portable-ladder-setup.formula: rail per foot of height at a b:1 setup = sqrt(1 + 1/b^2); base setback = height / b; rail to the landing = height x that factor; total rail = (height + 3 ft) x that factor; the highest landing served = ladder length / factor - 3 ft. Rung spacing must fall between 10 and 14 in between centrelines; clear width between side rails must be at least 11.5 in; side rails must extend at least 3 ft above the landing unless the ladder is secured at its top to a rigid support with a grasping device provided.
portable-ladder-setup.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1053, Subpart X - Stairways and Ladders. A US federal regulation in the public domain, quoted directly. The rail-budget arithmetic is geometry from the setup ratio, not a code value.
portable-ladder-setup.freeAccess: 29 CFR is published in full at no cost by OSHA and the eCFR.
portable-ladder-setup.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
portable-ladder-setup.editionNote: The 3 ft extension is a rule everyone knows and almost nobody costs out. It comes out of the CLIMBABLE length, and so does the setback: at a 4:1 setup every foot of height consumes 1.0308 ft of rail, so a 24 ft ladder needs 25.8 ft of rail to put its rails 3 ft above a 22 ft landing and simply does not reach. The highest landing that ladder actually serves is about 20.3 ft. A ladder never reaches its label - the number on the side is rail length, not working height - and buying the ladder whose number matches the roof height is the classic mistake this tile exists to prevent. Where the 3 ft extension is genuinely impossible the standard offers an alternative rather than a waiver: the ladder shall be secured at its top to a rigid support that will not deflect, AND a grasping device shall be provided. Both, not either, and the tile treats a claim of the alternative as satisfying the rule while naming what it requires. Rung spacing is a WINDOW rather than a minimum - not less than 10 in nor more than 14 in between centrelines - so rungs that are too close fail as surely as rungs that are too far apart, because what the window protects is a climber's stride. The clear width between side rails for all portable ladders is at least 11.5 in. Not checked: the 4:1 angle itself, which the ladder-angle tile computes and which this only uses to work out the rail budget; the ladder's duty rating and the load on it; securing the base and the footing it stands on; fixed ladders and ladders on scaffolds; the prohibition on standing on the top step of a stepladder; overlap between the sections of an extension ladder, which the extension-ladder-overlap tile computes and which reduces usable length further still; electrical clearance and conductive side rails near energized lines; and inspection and removal of defective ladders. A screen, not a ladder plan; Subpart X and the competent person govern.

assumptions.name: Extension
assumptions.value: side rails at least 3 ft above the upper landing surface

assumptions.name: Alternative
assumptions.value: secured at the top to a rigid support AND a grasping device provided

assumptions.name: Rail budget
assumptions.value: geometry: rail per foot of height = sqrt(1 + 1/ratio^2)

assumptions.name: Rung spacing
assumptions.value: a window, 10 to 14 in between centrelines

assumptions.name: Clear width
assumptions.value: at least 11.5 in between side rails for all portable ladders

assumptions.name: Not checked
assumptions.value: angle, duty rating, base securing, fixed ladders, section overlap, electrical clearance

sprinkler-system-demand.formula: sprinkler_gpm = density x design_area; total_gpm = sprinkler_gpm + hose_gpm; volume_gal = total_gpm x duration_min.
sprinkler-system-demand.edition: NFPA 13 (Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems), 2022, by name; the density / design-area / hose / duration levers come from the hazard classification and the density-area curves.
sprinkler-system-demand.freeAccess: NFPA 13 is viewable free of charge through NFPA's online free-access reader; the density x area + hose x duration arithmetic is public.
sprinkler-system-demand.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
sprinkler-system-demand.editionNote: NFPA 13 (Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems), 2022: sprinkler demand = density x design area, total demand = sprinkler demand + inside/outside hose-stream allowance, stored volume = total demand x duration. The hazard-class defaults are editable: Light 0.10 gpm/ft^2 over 1,500 ft^2 with 100 gpm hose for 30 min; Ordinary Group 1 0.15 / 1,500 / 250 / 60-90; Ordinary Group 2 0.20 / 1,500 / 250 / 60-90. This is the area/density screening demand (not the NFPA 13 pipe-schedule method, which has its own supply table) - a full hydraulic calculation to the most-remote area including friction and elevation yields the governing demand and is a separate analysis; the density / area / duration come from the applicable NFPA 13 density-area curve for the actual commodity and storage arrangement; storage and special occupancies (ESFR, high-piled, in-rack) use their own criteria. A design aid, not a stamped hydraulic submittal - a qualified fire-protection engineer and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Hazard-class levers
assumptions.value: the density, design area, hose allowance, and duration all come from the hazard classification (Light 0.10/1,500/100/30; OH1 0.15/1,500/250/60-90; OH2 0.20/1,500/250/60-90), editable defaults

assumptions.name: Screening demand
assumptions.value: the area/density product is the area/density screening demand (not the NFPA 13 pipe-schedule method); the governing demand comes from a full most-remote-area hydraulic calculation with friction and elevation

assumptions.name: Ordinary occupancies
assumptions.value: storage and special occupancies (ESFR, high-piled, in-rack) use their own density / area / duration criteria, not these defaults

sprinkler-protection-area-for-supply.formula: sprinkler_gpm = available_supply_gpm - hose_gpm; max_design_area_ft2 = sprinkler_gpm / density. The NFPA 13 area/density demand solved for the area.
sprinkler-protection-area-for-supply.edition: NFPA 13 (Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems), 2022, by name, solved for the design area.
sprinkler-protection-area-for-supply.freeAccess: NFPA 13 is viewable free of charge through NFPA's online free-access reader; the arithmetic is public.
sprinkler-protection-area-for-supply.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
sprinkler-protection-area-for-supply.editionNote: The inverse of sprinkler-system-demand: with the hose-stream allowance taken off the top, the remaining supply divided by the design density is the largest hydraulic design area the water supply can serve. A lower density (a lighter hazard) or a smaller hose allowance lets the same supply cover more area. This is the area/density screen (not the NFPA 13 pipe-schedule method, which has its own supply table) - a full hydraulic calculation to the most-remote area, at the flowing pressure the supply can deliver including friction and elevation, is the governing analysis and is separate. A design aid, not a stamped hydraulic submittal; a qualified fire-protection engineer and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Hose taken off the top
assumptions.value: sprinkler flow = supply - hose; the remainder / density is the coverable area

assumptions.name: Screening demand
assumptions.value: the area/density product is the area/density screen (not the NFPA 13 pipe-schedule method); the governing area comes from a full most-remote-area hydraulic calculation at the supply's flowing pressure

assumptions.name: Density from hazard
assumptions.value: the design density comes from the applicable NFPA 13 density-area curve for the actual commodity and arrangement

ut-thickness-velocity.formula: thickness = velocity x round-trip transit time / 2. The velocity error is a PERCENTAGE, so its absolute effect scales with the wall being inspected; the thinnest wall that still reads at a retirement limit is limit x actual velocity / gauge velocity.
ut-thickness-velocity.edition: The ultrasonic pulse-echo thickness relation. Velocities are ENTERED (steel about 0.232 in/us, aluminium about 0.2490) because they vary with alloy, temperature and grain structure -- a published table is a starting point and not a calibration.
ut-thickness-velocity.freeAccess: One relation and two entered velocities.
ut-thickness-velocity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ut-thickness-velocity.editionNote: A thickness gauge is a TIMER: it multiplies a measured transit time by whatever velocity it was told, so a gauge calibrated on steel and used on aluminium reports a number that is precise, repeatable, documented and wrong by about 7%. The error scales with the wall, so an absolute figure computed at one thickness does not transfer to another -- 7% of a five-inch section is about three hundred forty thousandths and 7% of a half-inch wall is thirty-four. THE TWO DIRECTIONS ARE NOT EQUALLY DANGEROUS: a gauge reading low retires equipment early, and a gauge reading high leaves a wall in service that is already below its retirement limit with a report saying it passed. Coating in single-echo mode reads thick, again in the unsafe direction, and echo-to-echo removes it.

assumptions.name: Velocities are entered
assumptions.value: they vary with alloy, temperature and grain structure
assumptions.source: a calibration block of the actual material

assumptions.name: A gauge finds thickness under the probe
assumptions.value: a pit between readings is missed entirely

assumptions.name: Not a fitness-for-service assessment
assumptions.value: and it does not set a retirement limit

caz-depressurization-limit.formula: the zone passes when the measured worst-case depressurization is at or below the limit for the WEAKEST vent type present; limits are entered by appliance class, and the margin is limit minus measured.
caz-depressurization-limit.edition: The combustion appliance zone depressurization test as BPI and CAZ field protocol states it, with the limits ENTERED by appliance class because they differ between protocols and jurisdictions. It is a pressure screen: it does not measure spillage, draft, or carbon monoxide, all of which the full protocol requires.
caz-depressurization-limit.freeAccess: One comparison against an entered limit.
caz-depressurization-limit.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
caz-depressurization-limit.editionNote: The rule the arithmetic encodes is that the zone is judged by the WEAKEST appliance in it, so a zone can contain appliances that individually pass and still fail. A natural-draft water heater with a limit of a few pascals sitting alongside an induced-draft furnace governs the whole zone, and this is the test that must be resolved before any further air sealing -- tightening a house that already fails is how backdrafting becomes carbon monoxide exposure. Reducing the exhaust that causes the depressurization comes before makeup air, and replacing the weakest appliance with a sealed-combustion unit removes the problem rather than managing it.

assumptions.name: Net of base pressure
assumptions.value: the reading is the worst case LESS the base (house at rest) reading: base +1 Pa and worst case -3 Pa is a net -4 Pa, which fails a 3 Pa limit the raw reading passes; BPI puts direct vent and sealed combustion at -50 Pa and a mechanically assisted draft furnace or boiler vented alone at -15 Pa
assumptions.source: BPI Building Analyst Standard; CT DEEP Form 5

assumptions.name: Limits are entered by appliance class
assumptions.value: they differ between protocols and jurisdictions

assumptions.name: Worst case is a test condition
assumptions.value: every exhaust on, interior doors positioned to worsen it

assumptions.name: Not a spillage or CO test
assumptions.value: pressure only

variable-primary-bypass.formula: minimum per machine = design evaporator flow x the minimum fraction; combined minimum = that times the machines running; bypass = combined minimum minus system flow when the system falls below it; valve Cv = bypass gpm / sqrt(differential psi) at the differential the pumps develop at that low flow.
variable-primary-bypass.edition: The variable primary chilled water minimum-flow bypass as central-plant practice writes it. The evaporator minimum fraction is ENTERED from the chiller manufacturer, because it varies by machine and evaporator design. It does not model the control sequence, the sensor location the bypass modulates from, the check valve and flow measurement a variable primary plant needs, or the transient during a stage change, which is when low-flow trips actually happen.
variable-primary-bypass.freeAccess: One flow balance and one valve-sizing relation.
variable-primary-bypass.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
variable-primary-bypass.editionNote: The bypass protects the MACHINE rather than controlling temperature: below the evaporator's minimum the water goes laminar, heat transfer collapses, control becomes unstable, the low-temperature safety trips, and on some machines repeated low-flow operation damages tubes. The interaction with STAGING is arithmetic rather than judgment -- two chillers running have twice the minimum flow of one -- so a plant that stages up at low load and does not stage back down promptly circulates water that does no work at all. Valve sizing has one counter-intuitive turn: the worst bypass condition is near pump shutoff, so the differential is HIGH and the required Cv is SMALLER than a design-differential sizing suggests, and an oversized bypass valve controls badly at the small openings it lives at.

assumptions.name: The minimum fraction is entered
assumptions.value: it varies by machine and evaporator design

assumptions.name: No control sequence
assumptions.value: the sensor location and the modulation are the designer's

assumptions.name: Steady state
assumptions.value: the stage-change transient is when low-flow trips happen

yeast-pitch-rate.formula: cells = rate (million/mL/degP) x volume mL x degP, with degP = 259 - 259/SG; slurry = cells / (concentration x viability).
yeast-pitch-rate.edition: Customary pitch rates of 0.75 for ales and 1.5 for lagers. A viability count on the day of pitching governs.
yeast-pitch-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
yeast-pitch-rate.editionNote: The slurry volume hides viability: pitching by volume from a mark underpitches the moment the yeast ages, with nothing in the bucket looking different.

assumptions.name: Plato
assumptions.value: the 259 - 259/SG approximation

sandbag-levee-quantity.formula: bags per linear foot N = 1.5 H + 4.5 H^2 (H in ft; reproduces USACE Table 2.1 exactly: 6, 21, 45, 78, 120 at 1-5 ft); total bags = N x length, rounded up; sand tons = bags x fill weight / 2,000; base width = 3 H; 3 ft preferred and 5 ft practical height limits flagged.
sandbag-levee-quantity.edition: USACE St. Paul District, Flood Fight Handbook (2016), Sections 2.3 and 2.5 and Table 2.1, with the USACE sandbag guidance of about 40 lb of sand per bag. The local emergency manager and the USACE district govern.
sandbag-levee-quantity.freeAccess: The USACE Flood Fight Handbook is a free federal publication; the table is reproduced as its exact quadratic fit.
sandbag-levee-quantity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
sandbag-levee-quantity.editionNote: A sandbag levee is a pyramid, so its cross-section grows with the square of its height, and the handbook's table of bags per linear foot fits a cap term plus a triangular-body term exactly. Written as a formula it extends to any length and to intermediate heights without interpolation, and it shows why raising a levee is so expensive: the third foot costs 24 bags per foot and the fifth costs 42. The base is three times the height, so the footprint has to fit before bagging starts. Bags are filled one-half to two-thirds full, about 35 to 40 lb, and a heavier fill wears out a volunteer line. Above 5 ft sandbags are the wrong tool and an earth levee or a manufactured barrier is used.

assumptions.name: USACE cross-section
assumptions.value: a pyramid levee with a base of three times its height, Table 2.1 bags per foot

assumptions.name: Fill weight
assumptions.value: about 40 lb of sand per bag, one-half to two-thirds full

assumptions.name: Height limits
assumptions.value: 3 ft preferred maximum, 5 ft practical limit
